Journalism. The practice of gathering, investigating, and reporting factual information for public distribution through newspapers, magazines, broadcasts, and digital media. As both a profession and a cultural force, journalism has served as a watchdog on power, a vehicle for public discourse, and a shaper of collective understanding. Its legal protections, ethical standards, and economic models have continuously evolved to balance the public's right to information against competing interests like privacy, national security, and commercial viability.

Journalism emerged as a systematic practice during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries alongside print technology and mass literacy expansion. The penny press of the eighteen-thirties and forties democratized news by making newspapers affordable to ordinary readers rather than just elites. Over time, the profession developed codes of ethics emphasizing factual accuracy, source protection, and independence from political control and commercial influence. American journalism received constitutional protection through the First Amendment, and the 1964 Supreme Court case New York Times Co. v. Sullivan clarified that public criticism is protected speech. Investigative journalism emerged as a discipline in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, exposing corruption and injustice through detailed reporting. Digital technology and the internet have transformed journalism's business model, distribution methods, and competitive landscape since the nineteen-nineties. Ernest Hemingway and other writers used journalism training to develop economical, clear prose styles that influenced literary fiction. Through all these changes, journalism's fundamental role remains to hold power accountable and serve the public interest through factual reporting, though the profession continues to grapple with questions of business model sustainability and the relationship between speed and accuracy in an age of instant information.
